tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

---
name: new-web-repo-setup
description: >
  Scaffold a new web application repository following Ashley Childress's established
  conventions: autonomous stack selection (Next.js, SvelteKit, Vite, Django, Go, Rust),
  monorepo vs single-package, Lefthook hooks, Makefile, GHA CI (with SonarCloud) +
  Release Please, Cloud Run deployment, Polyform Shield license, CODEOWNERS, CLAUDE.md,
  and AGENTS.md.

  ALWAYS trigger this skill when the user says things like "scaffold a new repo",
  "set up a new project", "create a new web app", "initialize a new repository",
  "start a new project from scratch", "new repo setup", "repo template", "project scaffold",
  "help me set up a new codebase", or describes a new project idea and asks how to structure it.
  Trigger even for partial requests like "what should I put in a new repo?" or "set up my
  tooling for a new project". This skill makes stack decisions autonomously from the
  project description — it does not ask the user to choose.
user-invocable: true
---

Make every architecture decision yourself from the project description. Deliver the full
initial scaffold: directory structure, tooling config, CI/CD workflows, deploy scripts,
boilerplate. The user says what they are building; you decide how.

Stop at repo structure and config. No components, routes, or application logic unless asked.

## Step 1: Understand the project

Extract from the user's description:
- What the project does (domain, users, purpose)
- Whether it has meaningful server-side logic (auth, databases, AI, background jobs, APIs)
- Whether a separate backend is warranted or whether framework built-ins suffice
- Any explicit technology preferences stated by the user (honor these)
- Whether it's Cloud Run–targeted (look for GCP, Cloud Run, or containerized mentions)

**Only ask a question if the description is fundamentally ambiguous** — e.g., "I want to
build an app" with no further detail. For anything with enough context to reason about,
make a decision and state it with one sentence of reasoning. Don't ask for confirmation
on stack choices.

The one thing to ask if truly unclear: **what should `docs/` contain?** Structure depends
too much on the project to guess reliably.

---

## Step 2: Make Stack Decisions Autonomously

Read the signals from the description and pick from these options.

### Frontend

| Signal | Pick |
|---|---|
| React preference, SEO matters, SSR needed, or full-stack | **Next.js** |
| React preference, pure client-side SPA, no SSR | **Vite + React** |
| Svelte preference, routing or SSR needed | **SvelteKit** |
| Svelte preference, pure client-side | **Vite + Svelte** |
| No UI — API/service only | None |

Default to **Next.js** for React projects when in doubt (better long-term flexibility).
Default to **SvelteKit** for Svelte projects when in doubt.

### Backend

Only reach for a separate backend when the project genuinely needs it. Framework built-ins
(Next.js API routes, SvelteKit endpoints) are sufficient for simple data fetching, light
CRUD, and proxying. A separate backend earns its weight when you have:
- AI/LLM integrations with complex orchestration
- Non-trivial auth (multi-tenant, OAuth, session management beyond a simple JWT)
- Relational data models with migrations and ORM
- Background job queues or event-driven processing
- Performance-critical services where Python's GIL or JS's single-thread is a liability

| Signal | Pick |
|---|---|
| Python ecosystem fit, AI/ML, rapid CRUD, admin interface | **Django + uv** |
| High-throughput API, microservice, fast Docker build, simple concurrency | **Go (Gin or Chi)** |
| Performance-critical, memory-constrained, CPU-intensive, or WebAssembly target | **Rust (Axum)** |
| No significant backend logic | No separate backend |

**Go** is a great default for high-concurrency APIs where Django would be overkill.
**Rust** earns its complexity only when performance or memory safety is a first-class
requirement — not just because the backend "needs to be fast."

### Multi-Package vs Single-Package

- **Multi-package:** Frontend and backend coexist in the same repo and release together.
  Structure: `web/` + `api/` at repo root. No monorepo tooling (Turborepo) unless
  explicitly requested — a root Makefile coordinates both packages.
- **Single-package:** Frontend only, or backend only, or services that release independently.

### Deployment

- If the project signals Cloud Run (GCP, containerized, serverless, or no explicit platform):
  include `deploy.sh` and Dockerfiles (read `references/cloudrun-deploy.md`).
- If deployment platform is unclear: scaffold the Makefile `deploy` target as a stub
  with a comment to fill in, and note this in the output.

---

## Step 3: Look Up Current Versions (Mandatory Pre-Flight — Do Not Skip)

Run web searches to find the latest stable release for **every** versioned dependency and
GHA action the scaffold will use. This step gates all version decisions. Do not proceed
to Step 4 until searches are complete.

Reference files in this skill are maintained manually and go stale within days. Every
version number in every reference file is a **stale placeholder that illustrates shape,
not value.** Do not copy any version from reference files, from training data, or from
memory. Treat them as if they contain the string `"SEARCH_ME"` wherever a version appears.

### What to search

Search every item in the chosen stack before writing a single version number:

| Category | Search pattern |
|---|---|
| npm/pnpm packages | `<package-name> npm latest version YYYY` |
| GitHub Actions | `<owner>/<repo> github releases latest` |
| pip packages | `<package-name> pypi latest version` |
| Go modules | `<module-path> github releases latest` |
| Rust crates | `<crate-name> crates.io latest` |

### Node version

Templates write `node-version: <ACTIVE_LTS>`. Resolve it from the release schedule, never
from a template, a memory, or the version on this machine:

```bash
curl -s https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodejs/Release/main/schedule.json | node -e '
let s="";process.stdin.on("data",c=>s+=c).on("end",()=>{
  const j=JSON.parse(s), n=new Date();
  for (const [k,v] of Object.entries(j)) {
    if (new Date(v.end) <= n) continue;
    const lts = v.lts && new Date(v.lts) <= n;
    const maint = v.maintenance && new Date(v.maintenance) <= n;
    console.log(k.padEnd(5), lts ? (maint ? "Maintenance LTS" : "Active LTS")
      : (new Date(v.start) <= n ? "Current" : "Future"), "eol=" + v.end);
  }})'
```

Take the line labelled `Active LTS`. `Current` becomes the next Active LTS each October, so
a scaffold written just before that cutover is stale within weeks — check the date rather
than assuming.

Use the newest **Active LTS**. Maintenance LTS is not a default for a new repo — it is
already past the point where new work should target it. A line that has not reached its
`lts` date is Current, not LTS: choose it only when the user asks for it explicitly.

Set the same version in `.nvmrc`, `engines.node`, the Dockerfile base image, and every
workflow. They drift apart otherwise, and the drift is invisible until a build breaks.

### Items that always require a search

**npm/pnpm (JS/TS stacks):**
- Framework: `next`, `react`, `react-dom`, `svelte`, `@sveltejs/kit`, `@sveltejs/adapter-auto`, `@sveltejs/vite-plugin-svelte`, `vite`
- Testing: `vitest`, `@vitest/coverage-v8`, `@playwright/test`, `@testing-library/react`, `@testing-library/svelte`, `@testing-library/jest-dom`, `@testing-library/user-event`, `jsdom`
- Tooling: `eslint`, `prettier`, `typescript`, `@lhci/cli`, `pnpm` (for `packageManager` field)
- Types: `@types/node`, `@types/react`, `@types/react-dom`
- Commitlint: `@commitlint/cli`, `@commitlint/config-conventional`, `commitlint-plugin-rai` (unscoped as of v1 — do not add an org prefix)

**pip (Django/Python stacks):**
- `django`, `djangorestframework`, `django-cors-headers`, `python-dotenv`, `gunicorn`
- Dev: `pytest`, `pytest-django`, `pytest-cov`, `ruff`, `mypy`, `django-stubs`, `djangorestframework-stubs`

**GitHub Actions (required for every scaffold):**

Templates write `@vLATEST`, never a number. Resolve every one before the file is saved;
`@vLATEST` left in a workflow is a broken workflow, which is the point — a stale number
ships silently, a placeholder fails loudly.

`gh` answers this exactly and needs no web search:

```bash
for r in actions/checkout actions/setup-node actions/cache actions/upload-artifact; do
  printf '%-26s %s\n' "$r" "$(gh api "repos/$r/releases/latest" --jq .tag_name)"
done
```

Pin `actions/*` to the major from that tag: `v7.0.1` → `@v7`.

- `actions/checkout`, `actions/setup-node`, `actions/cache`, `actions/upload-artifact`
- Third-party actions below need the release tag **and** its commit SHA
- `pnpm/action-setup` — third-party: find latest release tag **and** commit SHA
- `googleapis/release-please-action` — third-party: find latest release tag **and** commit SHA
- `SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action` — third-party: find latest release tag **and** commit SHA
- `gitleaks/gitleaks-action` — third-party: find latest release tag **and** commit SHA
- `github/codeql-action` (init, autobuild, analyze) — third-party: find latest release tag **and** commit SHA
- `astral-sh/setup-uv` — third-party (Django only): find latest release tag **and** commit SHA

### SHA pinning for third-party actions

For every third-party action (anything not under `actions/*` or `github/*`), you need both
the tag and a commit SHA. Search the action's GitHub releases page to find the SHA that
corresponds to the latest release tag, then format it as:

```yaml
uses: owner/action@<full-commit-sha> # vX.Y.Z
```

Do not reuse SHA values from reference files — SHAs are tied to a specific commit and
the reference files are stale. Look up the actual SHA for the version you found in your search.

### If a search fails

Note the failure explicitly in your output. Fall back to the `latest` dist-tag or
`@main` with a comment: `# version could not be verified — check before committing`.
Never silently use a hardcoded value from a reference file or training memory.

---

## Step 4: Generate Files

Read the relevant reference files for **structure and configuration shape only** — not
for version numbers (those were resolved in Step 3). Output concrete file contents — every
file gets a labelled code block. Don't describe what a file should contain; write it.

### Always included (every repo)

Read `references/shared-templates.md` for structure (use Step 3 version lookups, not file versions):
- `LICENSE` — Polyform Shield 1.0.0 (Ashley Childress)
- `.github/CODEOWNERS` — `* @anchildress1`
- `CLAUDE.md` — minimal, references AGENTS.md
- `AGENTS.md` — filled with project-specific rules
- `README.md` — project name, description, setup + dev commands
- **`Makefile`** ← **strictly required**: must include targets `install`, `dev`, `format`,
  `format-check`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `test`, `build`, `e2e`, `perf`, `secret-scan`,
  `clean`. Add stack-appropriate commands. Never omit or rename these targets.
- `lefthook.yml` — pre-commit (format → lint → scan-secrets) + commit-msg (commitlint
  with RAI plugin) + pre-push (parallel: typecheck, unit tests, E2E, perf). Adapt
  commands to stack.
- `commitlint.config.js` — extends `@commitlint/config-conventional` with
  `commitlint-plugin-rai` (unscoped as of v1 — no org prefix) for RAI attribution
  enforcement.
- `.prettierignore` — always exclude `**/CHANGELOG.md` (release-please-generated; formatting
  it fights the tool every release) plus the stack's build/output dirs. Use the glob, not a
  bare filename, so package changelogs in a monorepo are covered too.
- `eslint.config.js` — flat config. Always include `**/CHANGELOG.md` in `ignores`, alongside
  the stack's build/output dirs. Inert while the config only matches source globs, and it
  keeps release-please's file untouched the moment a markdown processor is added.
- `sonar-project.properties` — SonarCloud config. The `sonar.projectKey` and
  `sonar.organization` are provided by the user — **ask if not given**. Adapt sources,
  test inclusions, and coverage report paths to the stack.

Read `references/gha-templates.md` for workflow structure (use Step 3 version lookups for all action refs and SHAs):
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — format check, lint, build, unit tests,
  SonarCloud (always in CI, not a separate workflow), E2E, Lighthouse, secret scan,
  artifact uploads
- `.github/workflows/codeql.yml` — CodeQL semantic analysis (adapt language matrix to stack)
- `.github/workflows/release-please.yml`
- `.github/dependabot.yml` — see `references/shared-templates.md` §`.github/dependabot.yml`.
  Two grouped ecosystems (GitHub Actions + the stack's package manager), 1 open PR
  per ecosystem, schedules staggered (gha Monday, pkg Thursday) so the two PRs
  rarely overlap.

### Stack-specific files

**Next.js** → read `references/nextjs-config.md` for structure (substitute Step 3 versions):
- `package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `next.config.ts`, `vitest.config.ts`,
  `playwright.config.ts`, `.lighthouserc.json`

**Svelte** → read `references/svelte-config.md` for structure (substitute Step 3 versions):
- `package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `svelte.config.ts` or `vite.config.ts`,
  `vitest.config.ts`, `playwright.config.ts`, `.lighthouserc.json`

**Django** → read `references/django-config.md` for structure (substitute Step 3 versions):
- `pyproject.toml`, `ruff.toml`, Django project skeleton, `conftest.py`

**Go** → scaffold these (no reference file yet — generate from first principles; search for
current Go LTS version and distroless image tag in Step 3):
- `go.mod` with module path and current Go LTS version (from Step 3 search)
- `main.go` with a minimal HTTP server skeleton (Gin or Chi)
- `Makefile` Go targets: `go build ./...`, `go test ./...`, `go vet ./...`
- `Dockerfile`: current `golang:<version>-bookworm` builder → `gcr.io/distroless/base` runner
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` Go steps: `go vet`, `golangci-lint`, `go test -race ./...`

**Rust** → scaffold these (no reference file yet — generate from first principles; search for
current Rust stable version and base image in Step 3):
- `Cargo.toml` with Axum, Tokio, and common deps (serde, tracing, anyhow) — search crates.io for
  current versions
- `src/main.rs` with a minimal Axum server skeleton
- `Makefile` Rust targets: `cargo build`, `cargo test`, `cargo clippy`, `cargo fmt`
- `Dockerfile`: current `rust:<version>-bookworm` builder → `debian:bookworm-slim` runner
  (distroless if statically linked)
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` Rust steps: `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`,
  `cargo test`

**Multi-package repos** → additionally include:
- Root `Makefile` with targets that delegate to both `web/` and `api/`
- Per-package configs nested under `web/` and `api/`
- `.npmrc` in `web/` (`shamefully-hoist=false`)

**Cloud Run deployment** → read `references/cloudrun-deploy.md` for structure (substitute Step 3 versions for any image tags or versions):
- **`deploy.sh`** ← **strictly required for Cloud Run projects**: always include this
- `web/Dockerfile` (frontend variant)
- `web/cloudbuild.yaml` (if Next.js, for build arg injection)
- `api/Dockerfile` (Django, FastAPI, Go, or Rust variant)
- `.dockerignore` files

---

## Step 5: Output Format

Open with a one-sentence stack decision rationale. Then:

```
## Repository Structure
<tree view of all files>

## Files

### Makefile
\`\`\`makefile
...
\`\`\`

### lefthook.yml
...

[one labelled code block per file, in order: root config → .github/ → stack config → deploy]
```

After outputting, offer to write any of these files directly to disk.

---

## Defaults and Preferences

These are the preferred starting points. They can be overridden by explicit user instruction.

| Concern | Preferred default |
|---|---|
| Node version manager | Volta |
| Node version | 22+ |
| Python version | 3.13 |
| JS package manager | pnpm |
| Python package manager | uv |
| TypeScript | `strict: true` |
| Frontend test runner | Vitest + Playwright |
| Coverage thresholds | 85% lines/functions/statements, 80% branches |
| Lighthouse (mobile) | 90% performance |
| Lighthouse (desktop) | 100% performance |
| Lighthouse (a11y/SEO/BP) | 95% |

## Step 6: Commit Layout (non-negotiable)

The scaffold is a pull request, never the first commit.

- Initial commit on `main`: `README.md`, `LICENSE`, `.gitignore` — nothing else.
- Everything else generated by Step 4 — build files, dependencies, CI, app code — lands on a
  branch and is opened as a PR against that bare `main`.
- A 10-commit "initial scaffold" squashed onto `main` is not an initial commit. There is no
  version of this that is acceptable.

Rationale, because this looks like ceremony and is not: a repo whose history starts with the
whole scaffold has no reviewable diff for any of it. Every later "why is this configured this
way" question resolves to one opaque commit.

## Hard Requirements (never skip)

- **Version lookups via web search** before writing any version number — no exceptions.
  Reference files, training data, and memory are all prohibited sources for versions.
- **Makefile** with the exact target names listed in Step 4
- **`deploy.sh`** + Dockerfiles when the project deploys to Cloud Run
- **`LICENSE`** — Polyform Shield 1.0.0
- **`.github/CODEOWNERS`** — `* @anchildress1`
- **`.github/dependabot.yml`** — two grouped ecosystems (GHA + package manager), 1 open
  PR per ecosystem, schedules staggered (gha Monday, pkg Thursday), and
  `cooldown.default-days: 7` on **every** entry (supply-chain guard; Semgrep flags its
  absence). Bun repos use `package-ecosystem: bun`, never `npm`.
- **SonarCloud** inside the CI workflow (never a separate workflow)
- **CodeQL** workflow (`codeql.yml`) with language matrix adapted to stack
- **actionlint** in lefthook pre-commit hook (NOT in CI — runs locally only)
- **Release Please** always scaffolded
- **Bare initial commit** — README + LICENSE + .gitignore only; scaffold arrives by PR (Step 6)
- **pnpm** as the package manager for every JS/TS stack — never npm or yarn (lockfile,
  Makefile, CI, and lefthook commands all use pnpm). Only deviate on explicit user override.

- Performance-critical services where Python's GIL or JS's single-thread is a liability

| Signal | Pick |
|---|---|
| Python ecosystem fit, AI/ML, rapid CRUD, admin interface | **Django + uv** |
| High-throughput API, microservice, fast Docker build, simple concurrency | **Go (Gin or Chi)** |
| Performance-critical, memory-constrained, CPU-intensive, or WebAssembly target | **Rust (Axum)** |
| No significant backend logic | No separate backend |

**Go** is a great default for high-concurrency APIs where Django would be overkill.
**Rust** earns its complexity only when performance or memory safety is a first-class
requirement — not just because the backend "needs to be fast."

### Multi-Package vs Single-Package

- **Multi-package:** Frontend and backend coexist in the same repo and release together.
  Structure: `web/` + `api/` at repo root. No monorepo tooling (Turborepo) unless
  explicitly requested — a root Makefile coordinates both packages.
- **Single-package:** Frontend only, or backend only, or services that release independently.

### Deployment

- If the project signals Cloud Run (GCP, containerized, serverless, or no explicit platform):
  include `deploy.sh` and Dockerfiles (read `references/cloudrun-deploy.md`).
- If deployment platform is unclear: scaffold the Makefile `deploy` target as a stub
  with a comment to fill in, and note this in the output.

---

## Step 3: Look Up Current Versions (Mandatory Pre-Flight — Do Not Skip)

Run web searches to find the latest stable release for **every** versioned dependency and
GHA action the scaffold will use. This step gates all version decisions. Do not proceed
to Step 4 until searches are complete.

Reference files in this skill are maintained manually and go stale within days. Every
version number in every reference file is a **stale placeholder that illustrates shape,
not value.** Do not copy any version from reference files, from training data, or from
memory. Treat them as if they contain the string `"SEARCH_ME"` wherever a version appears.

### What to search

Search every item in the chosen stack before writing a single version number:

| Category | Search pattern |
|---|---|
| npm/pnpm packages | `<package-name> npm latest version YYYY` |
| GitHub Actions | `<owner>/<repo> github releases latest` |
| pip packages | `<package-name> pypi latest version` |
| Go modules | `<module-path> github releases latest` |
| Rust crates | `<crate-name> crates.io latest` |

### Node version

Templates write `node-version: <ACTIVE_LTS>`. Resolve it from the release schedule, never
from a template, a memory, or the version on this machine:

```bash
curl -s https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodejs/Release/main/schedule.json | node -e '
let s="";process.stdin.on("data",c=>s+=c).on("end",()=>{
  const j=JSON.parse(s), n=new Date();
  for (const [k,v] of Object.entries(j)) {
    if (new Date(v.end) <= n) continue;
    const lts = v.lts && new Date(v.lts) <= n;
    const maint = v.maintenance && new Date(v.maintenance) <= n;
    console.log(k.padEnd(5), lts ? (maint ? "Maintenance LTS" : "Active LTS")
      : (new Date(v.start) <= n ? "Current" : "Future"), "eol=" + v.end);
  }})'
```

Take the line labelled `Active LTS`. `Current` becomes the next Active LTS each October, so
a scaffold written just before that cutover is stale within weeks — check the date rather
than assuming.

Use the newest **Active LTS**. Maintenance LTS is not a default for a new repo — it is
already past the point where new work should target it. A line that has not reached its
`lts` date is Current, not LTS: choose it only when the user asks for it explicitly.

Set the same version in `.nvmrc`, `engines.node`, the Dockerfile base image, and every
workflow. They drift apart otherwise, and the drift is invisible until a build breaks.

### Items that always require a search

**npm/pnpm (JS/TS stacks):**
- Framework: `next`, `react`, `react-dom`, `svelte`, `@sveltejs/kit`, `@sveltejs/adapter-auto`, `@sveltejs/vite-plugin-svelte`, `vite`
- Testing: `vitest`, `@vitest/coverage-v8`, `@playwright/test`, `@testing-library/react`, `@testing-library/svelte`, `@testing-library/jest-dom`, `@testing-library/user-event`, `jsdom`
- Tooling: `eslint`, `prettier`, `typescript`, `@lhci/cli`, `pnpm` (for `packageManager` field)
- Types: `@types/node`, `@types/react`, `@types/react-dom`
- Commitlint: `@commitlint/cli`, `@commitlint/config-conventional`, `commitlint-plugin-rai` (unscoped as of v1 — do not add an org prefix)

**pip (Django/Python stacks):**
- `django`, `djangorestframework`, `django-cors-headers`, `python-dotenv`, `gunicorn`
- Dev: `pytest`, `pytest-django`, `pytest-cov`, `ruff`, `mypy`, `django-stubs`, `djangorestframework-stubs`

**GitHub Actions (required for every scaffold):**

Templates write `@vLATEST`, never a number. Resolve every one before the file is saved;
`@vLATEST` left in a workflow is a broken workflow, which is the point — a stale number
ships silently, a placeholder fails loudly.

`gh` answers this exactly and needs no web search:

```bash
for r in actions/checkout actions/setup-node actions/cache actions/upload-artifact; do
  printf '%-26s %s\n' "$r" "$(gh api "repos/$r/releases/latest" --jq .tag_name)"
done
```

Pin `actions/*` to the major from that tag: `v7.0.1` → `@v7`.

- `actions/checkout`, `actions/setup-node`, `actions/cache`, `actions/upload-artifact`
- Third-party actions below need the release tag **and** its commit SHA
- `pnpm/action-setup` — third-party: find latest release tag **and** commit SHA
- `googleapis/release-please-action` — third-party: find latest release tag **and** commit SHA
- `SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action` — third-party: find latest release tag **and** commit SHA
- `gitleaks/gitleaks-action` — third-party: find latest release tag **and** commit SHA
- `github/codeql-action` (init, autobuild, analyze) — third-party: find latest release tag **and** commit SHA
- `astral-sh/setup-uv` — third-party (Django only): find latest release tag **and** commit SHA

### SHA pinning for third-party actions

For every third-party action (anything not under `actions/*` or `github/*`), you need both
the tag and a commit SHA. Search the action's GitHub releases page to find the SHA that
corresponds to the latest release tag, then format it as:

```yaml
uses: owner/action@<full-commit-sha> # vX.Y.Z
```

Do not reuse SHA values from reference files — SHAs are tied to a specific commit and
the reference files are stale. Look up the actual SHA for the version you found in your search.

### If a search fails

Note the failure explicitly in your output. Fall back to the `latest` dist-tag or
`@main` with a comment: `# version could not be verified — check before committing`.
Never silently use a hardcoded value from a reference file or training memory.

---

## Step 4: Generate Files

Read the relevant reference files for **structure and configuration shape only** — not
for version numbers (those were resolved in Step 3). Output concrete file contents — every
file gets a labelled code block. Don't describe what a file should contain; write it.

### Always included (every repo)

Read `references/shared-templates.md` for structure (use Step 3 version lookups, not file versions):
- `LICENSE` — Polyform Shield 1.0.0 (Ashley Childress)
- `.github/CODEOWNERS` — `* @anchildress1`
- `CLAUDE.md` — minimal, references AGENTS.md
- `AGENTS.md` — filled with project-specific rules
- `README.md` — project name, description, setup + dev commands
- **`Makefile`** ← **strictly required**: must include targets `install`, `dev`, `format`,
  `format-check`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `test`, `build`, `e2e`, `perf`, `secret-scan`,
  `clean`. Add stack-appropriate commands. Never omit or rename these targets.
- `lefthook.yml` — pre-commit (format → lint → scan-secrets) + commit-msg (commitlint
  with RAI plugin) + pre-push (parallel: typecheck, unit tests, E2E, perf). Adapt
  commands to stack.
- `commitlint.config.js` — extends `@commitlint/config-conventional` with
  `commitlint-plugin-rai` (unscoped as of v1 — no org prefix) for RAI attribution
  enforcement.
- `.prettierignore` — always exclude `**/CHANGELOG.md` (release-please-generated; formatting
  it fights the tool every release) plus the stack's build/output dirs. Use the glob, not a
  bare filename, so package changelogs in a monorepo are covered too.
- `eslint.config.js` — flat config. Always include `**/CHANGELOG.md` in `ignores`, alongside
  the stack's build/output dirs. Inert while the config only matches source globs, and it

- `sonar-project.properties` — SonarCloud config. The `sonar.projectKey` and

Read `references/gha-templates.md` for workflow structure (use Step 3 version lookups for all action refs and SHAs):
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — format check, lint, build, unit tests,

- `.github/workflows/codeql.yml` — CodeQL semantic analysis (adapt language matrix to stack)
- `.github/workflows/release-please.yml`
- `.github/dependabot.yml` — see `references/shared-templates.md` §`.github/dependabot.yml`.
  Two grouped ecosystems (GitHub Actions + the stack's package manager), 1 open PR
  per ecosystem, schedules staggered (gha Monday, pkg Thursday) so the two PRs
  rarely overlap.

### Stack-specific files

**Next.js** → read `references/nextjs-config.md` for structure (substitute Step 3 versions):
- `package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `next.config.ts`, `vitest.config.ts`,

**Svelte** → read `references/svelte-config.md` for structure (substitute Step 3 versions):
- `package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `svelte.config.ts` or `vite.config.ts`,
  `vitest.config.ts`, `playwright.config.ts`, `.lighthouserc.json`

**Django** → read `references/django-config.md` for structure (substitute Step 3 versions):
- `pyproject.toml`, `ruff.toml`, Django project skeleton, `conftest.py`

**Go** → scaffold these (no reference file yet — generate from first principles; search for
current Go LTS version and distroless image tag in Step 3):
- `go.mod` with module path and current Go LTS version (from Step 3 search)
- `main.go` with a minimal HTTP server skeleton (Gin or Chi)

- `Dockerfile`: current `golang:<version>-bookworm` builder → `gcr.io/distroless/base` runner
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` Go steps: `go vet`, `golangci-lint`, `go test -race ./...`

**Rust** → scaffold these (no reference file yet — generate from first principles; search for
current Rust stable version and base image in Step 3):
- `Cargo.toml` with Axum, Tokio, and common deps (serde, tracing, anyhow) — search crates.io for
  current versions
- `src/main.rs` with a minimal Axum server skeleton
- `Makefile` Rust targets: `cargo build`, `cargo test`, `cargo clippy`, `cargo fmt`
- `Dockerfile`: current `rust:<version>-bookworm` builder → `debian:bookworm-slim` runner
  (distroless if statically linked)
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` Rust steps: `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`,
  `cargo test`

**Multi-package repos** → additionally include:
- Root `Makefile` with targets that delegate to both `web/` and `api/`
- Per-package configs nested under `web/` and `api/`
- `.npmrc` in `web/` (`shamefully-hoist=false`)

**Cloud Run deployment** → read `references/cloudrun-deploy.md` for structure (substitute Step 3 versions for any image tags or versions):
- **`deploy.sh`** ← **strictly required for Cloud Run projects**: always include this

Open with a one-sentence stack decision rationale. Then:

```
## Repository Structure
<tree view of all files>

## Files

### Makefile
\`\`\`makefile
...
\`\`\`

### lefthook.yml
...

[one labelled code block per file, in order: root config → .github/ → stack config → deploy]
```

After outputting, offer to write any of these files directly to disk.

---

## Defaults and Preferences

These are the preferred starting points. They can be overridden by explicit user instruction.

| Concern | Preferred default |
|---|---|
| Node version manager | Volta |
| Node version | 22+ |
| Python version | 3.13 |
| JS package manager | pnpm |
| Python package manager | uv |
| TypeScript | `strict: true` |
| Frontend test runner | Vitest + Playwright |
| Coverage thresholds | 85% lines/functions/statements, 80% branches |
| Lighthouse (mobile) | 90% performance |
| Lighthouse (desktop) | 100% performance |
| Lighthouse (a11y/SEO/BP) | 95% |

## Step 6: Commit Layout (non-negotiable)

The scaffold is a pull request, never the first commit.

- Initial commit on `main`: `README.md`, `LICENSE`, `.gitignore` — nothing else.
- Everything else generated by Step 4 — build files, dependencies, CI, app code — lands on a
  branch and is opened as a PR against that bare `main`.
- A 10-commit "initial scaffold" squashed onto `main` is not an initial commit. There is no
  version of this that is acceptable.

Rationale, because this looks like ceremony and is not: a repo whose history starts with the
whole scaffold has no reviewable diff for any of it. Every later "why is this configured this
way" question resolves to one opaque commit.

## Hard Requirements (never skip)

- **Version lookups via web search** before writing any version number — no exceptions.
  Reference files, training data, and memory are all prohibited sources for versions.
- **Makefile** with the exact target names listed in Step 4
- **`deploy.sh`** + Dockerfiles when the project deploys to Cloud Run
- **`LICENSE`** — Polyform Shield 1.0.0
- **`.github/CODEOWNERS`** — `* @anchildress1`
- **`.github/dependabot.yml`** — two grouped ecosystems (GHA + package manager), 1 open
  PR per ecosystem, schedules staggered (gha Monday, pkg Thursday), and
  `cooldown.default-days: 7` on **every** entry (supply-chain guard; Semgrep flags its
  absence). Bun repos use `package-ecosystem: bun`, never `npm`.
- **SonarCloud** inside the CI workflow (never a separate workflow)
- **CodeQL** workflow (`codeql.yml`) with language matrix adapted to stack
- **actionlint** in lefthook pre-commit hook (NOT in CI — runs locally only)
- **Release Please** always scaffolded
- **Bare initial commit** — README + LICENSE + .gitignore only; scaffold arrives by PR (Step 6)
- **pnpm** as the package manager for every JS/TS stack — never npm or yarn (lockfile,
  Makefile, CI, and lefthook commands all use pnpm). Only deviate on explicit user override.

The most recent Node.js 26 security release I found is from October 21, 2026, and it fixed the Current line at 26.12.1.

- **October 2026 release:** HKCERT's October 22 bulletin lists affected versions as anything before 22.23.4 (LTS), 24.22.1 (LTS), and 26.12.1 (Current), and it warns of possible denial of service, remote code execution, information disclosure, and security restriction bypass. The October 21 Node.js security release fixes are 26.12.1, 24.22.1 and 22.23.4. That second source is a third-party blog, so the official Node.js release notes or security advisory are the authority to confirm against.
- **Earlier 2026 releases:** HKCERT also issued bulletins for Node.js versions prior to 26.3.1 (Current) in June and Node.js versions prior to 26.5.1 (Current) in July.
- **Individual CVE:** Vulert's entry for CVE-2026-56848 describes a heap use-after-free in HTTP/2 handling that affects Node.js versions 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x. The page has no date, so I can't tie it to October. Its suggested workaround is to consider disabling HTTP/2 support in your Node.js application until you can upgrade to a patched version.
- **Caveat on Red Hat advisories:** Vulert's Red Hat advisory pages for nodejs26 are dated June and June 27, 2026, so they predate the October release and only matter if you run the Red Hat packages.

Upgrading to 26.12.1 is the fix for the October release. I didn't find the official nodejs.org advisory for October in these results.

MVP proof of concept. Hard deadline: 2026-10-31 23:59 PDT. Ship the smallest thing that satisfies `docs/PRD.md`.

## Scope

- Build only what the MVP journey in `docs/PRD.md` requires. Anything outside it: stop and ask.
- No feature flags, plugin systems, config layers, caching, retries, queues, or i18n unless a broken user path demands it.
- Prefer a framework/library capability over hand-rolled code.
- Delete dead code. Never keep a path "just in case". No backward-compat shims.
- Exactly two abstraction seams exist: **model inference** and **historical search**. One interface each, one implementation each until a second is actually needed. Concrete classes everywhere else.

## Design

- Follow SOLID, KISS, YAGNI at all times. When they conflict, KISS and YAGNI win.
- One responsibility per module. No god files, no `utils` dumping grounds.
- Never fabricate history. Every narrative claim maps to a source record; unsupported fields render as unknown, not guessed.
- Never merge records from different people silently. Ambiguous identity → return candidates for user confirmation.

## Tests

- Test functional logic only: inscription parsing, identity matching, claim-to-source mapping, input validation, narrative grounding checks.
- Never write a test whose purpose is coverage. Banned: tests of constants, type shapes, getters, framework wiring, rendering-only snapshots, mocks asserting they were called.
- Mock at the network boundary (Gemini API, SerpApi, ElevenLabs). Never hit live APIs in tests.
- Bug fix → one test that fails before the fix.

## Comments and JSDoc

- Inline comments: only to explain **why** a decision was made. Otherwise omit.
- JSDoc is required on every function, method, and class — exported or not.
- JSDoc format: one-line summary, `@param`, `@returns`, `@throws` when applicable. Do not restate types TypeScript already declares.

```ts
/**
 * Scores how likely a search hit refers to the person on the headstone.
 * @param inscription Fields extracted from the headstone image.
 * @param hit Candidate record from historical search.
 * @returns Confidence in [0, 1].
 */
```

## Toolchain

- Node **26.12.1** exactly. Earlier 26.x releases carry the CVEs fixed in the 2026-10-21 security release. Pin the same version in `package.json` (`engines`, `volta`), the Dockerfile, and CI. Never lower it.
- TypeScript `strict`. ESM only. No CommonJS.
- pnpm only. Never npm or yarn.
- Lint, type, and test warnings are errors.
- Secrets live in `.env` only (gitignored). `.env.example` lists keys with empty values.

# 🪦 Gravespeaker

**Every stone has a story. Let it speak.**

*Photograph a headstone. Discover a life. Hear the story the records left behind.*

**Project:** Hacktoberfest 2026, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine
**Deadline:** October 31, 2026, 11:59 PM PDT
**Status:** MVP in development

## 1. Vision

Gravespeaker is a mobile-friendly web application that brings historical lives back into focus.

Users photograph a gravestone or upload an existing image. AI extracts identifying details, searches publicly accessible historical records, and reconstructs the deceased person's story in first person, as though they're speaking from beyond the grave.

The experience should feel mysterious and personal while remaining historically responsible.

**Core principle:** Resurrect the story, not invent the person.

## 2. MVP User Journey

| # | Step | What happens | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Capture or upload** | Photograph a gravestone or select an existing image. | Works from a phone camera and from a desktop file picker. |
| 2 | **Identify** | AI extracts names, dates, inscriptions and other useful details. | User can review and correct every extracted field before searching. |
| 3 | **Research** | Search obituaries, cemetery records, historical archives and indexed public information. | Results come back with source URLs attached. |
| 4 | **Verify** | Cross-reference names, dates and places. | When more than one plausible person matches, the user picks one (or none). |
| 5 | **Resurrect** | Generate a short first-person narrative grounded in the confirmed records. | Every factual sentence links to at least one source. |
| 6 | **Explore** | Show source links and separate documented facts from AI reconstruction. | Facts and reconstruction are visually distinct, and the narrative is labelled as AI-generated. |

If credible information can't be found, the app says so. It never fills historical gaps with fabricated claims.

## 3. Technical Direction

| Component | Choice |
|---|---|
| Frontend | Svelte + Vite, responsive web |
| Backend | Node.js 26 / TypeScript |
| AI orchestration | Mastra |
| Vision and OCR | Gemma 4 via Google Gemini API |
| Historical search | SerpApi |
| Narrative generation | Gemma 4 |
| Hosting | Google Cloud Run |
| Optional narration | ElevenLabs |
| Builder | Claude Code |
| Development tracking | Entire |

Model inference and historical search sit behind replaceable interfaces. Everything else stays concrete.

No self-hosted models unless benchmarks show a compelling advantage.

## 4. Key Engineering Challenges

**Headstone recognition**
- Weathered stone, damaged inscriptions, shadows, unusual typography and partial dates.
- Measure actual recognition accuracy instead of assuming a vision model performs well.

**Historical identity resolution**
- Common names, incomplete records, contradictory dates and similarly named people.
- Use multiple identity signals (name, birth/death dates, location) and make uncertainty explicit.
- Never silently combine different people's histories.

**Source discovery and reliability**
- Public availability doesn't guarantee unrestricted reuse.
- Respect access restrictions, provenance, licensing and unavailable records. Link to sources; don't republish their content.
- Every substantive historical claim must trace back to supporting evidence.

**First-person storytelling**
- Atmospheric and engaging without inventing relationships, events, memories, thoughts or emotions.
- Clearly label narratives as AI-generated historical reconstructions.
- Leave out unnecessary sensitive details about living people (for example, surviving relatives named in obituaries).

**Model selection**
- Benchmark Gemma 4 against a closed Gemini model on identical test inputs.
- Compare OCR accuracy, factual grounding, unsupported claims, latency and cost.
- Consider a specialised open OCR model only if testing justifies the extra integration.

## 5. Open Innovation and Challenge Alignment

The open-weight model has to meaningfully contribute to the finished app, not exist only for challenge eligibility.

**Thesis for the DEV post:**

> The value of open innovation isn't that we refused to use closed AI. It's that we could independently test, choose, and improve the technology instead of accepting one provider's answer as the only option.

Document where the open approach performs better, matches a closed alternative, or exposes tradeoffs. Back conclusions with real benchmarks and reproducible examples.

The post focuses on the problem, engineering decisions, real discoveries, failure cases, and the value of making forgotten histories more accessible.

## 6. Scope Boundaries

**Required**
- Functional mobile-friendly website covering the full MVP journey in §2.

**Out of scope for the MVP**
- User accounts, saved history, or any persistent storage of uploaded images.
- Self-hosted model inference.
- Paywalled or login-gated record sources.

## 7. Privacy

- Uploaded images are processed in memory and not stored.
- API keys stay server-side. The browser never talls a model or search provider directly.

# 🪦 Gravespeaker

**Every stone has a story. Let it speak.**

*Photograph a headstone. Discover a life. Hear the story the records left behind.*

**Project:** Hacktoberfest 2026, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine
**Deadline:** October 31, 2026, 11:59 PM PDT
**Status:** MVP in development

## 1. Vision

Gravespeaker is a mobile-friendly web application that brings historical lives back into focus.

Users photograph a gravestone or upload an existing image. AI extracts identifying details, searches publicly accessible historical records, and reconstructs the deceased person's story in first person, as though they're speaking from beyond the grave.

The experience should feel mysterious and personal while remaining historically responsible.

**Core principle:** Resurrect the story, not invent the person.

## 2. MVP User Journey

| # | Step | What happens | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Capture or upload** | Photograph a gravestone or select an existing image. | Works from a phone camera and from a desktop file picker. |
| 2 | **Identify** | AI extracts names, dates, inscriptions and other useful details. | User can review and correct every extracted field before searching. |
| 3 | **Research** | Search obituaries, cemetery records, historical archives and indexed public information. | Results come back with source URLs attached. |
| 4 | **Verify** | Cross-reference names, dates and places. | When more than one plausible person matches, the user picks one (or none). |
| 5 | **Resurrect** | Generate a short first-person narrative grounded in the confirmed records. | Every factual sentence links to at least one source. |
| 6 | **Explore** | Show source links and separate documented facts from AI reconstruction. | Facts and reconstruction are visually distinct, and the narrative is labelled as AI-generated. |

If credible information can't be found, the app says so. It never fills historical gaps with fabricated claims.

## 3. Technical Direction

| Component | Choice |
|---|---|
| Frontend | Svelte + Vite, responsive web |
| Backend | Node.js 26 / TypeScript |
| AI orchestration | Mastra |
| Vision and OCR | Gemma 4 via Google Gemini API |
| Historical search | SerpApi |
| Narrative generation | Gemma 4 |
| Hosting | Google Cloud Run |
| Optional narration | ElevenLabs |
| Builder | Claude Code |
| Development tracking | Entire |

Model inference and historical search sit behind replaceable interfaces. Everything else stays concrete.

No self-hosted models unless benchmarks show a compelling advantage.

## 4. Key Engineering Challenges

**Headstone recognition**
- Weathered stone, damaged inscriptions, shadows, unusual typography and partial dates.
- Measure actual recognition accuracy instead of assuming a vision model performs well.

**Historical identity resolution**
- Common names, incomplete records, contradictory dates and similarly named people.
- Use multiple identity signals (name, birth/death dates, location) and make uncertainty explicit.
- Never silently combine different people's histories.

**Source discovery and reliability**
- Public availability doesn't guarantee unrestricted reuse.
- Respect access restrictions, provenance, licensing and unavailable records. Link to sources; don't republish their content.
- Every substantive historical claim must trace back to supporting evidence.

**First-person storytelling**
- Atmospheric and engaging without inventing relationships, events, memories, thoughts or emotions.
- Clearly label narratives as AI-generated historical reconstructions.
- Leave out unnecessary sensitive details about living people (for example, surviving relatives named in obituaries).

**Model selection**
- Benchmark Gemma 4 against a closed Gemini model on identical test inputs.
- Compare OCR accuracy, factual grounding, unsupported claims, latency and cost.
- Consider a specialised open OCR model only if testing justifies the extra integration.

## 5. Open Innovation and Challenge Alignment

The open-weight model has to meaningfully contribute to the finished app, not exist only for challenge eligibility.

**Thesis for the DEV post:**

> The value of open innovation isn't that we refused to use closed AI. It's that we could independently test, choose, and improve the technology instead of accepting one provider's answer as the only option.

Document where the open approach performs better, matches a closed alternative, or exposes tradeoffs. Back conclusions with real benchmarks and reproducible examples.

The post focuses on the problem, engineering decisions, real discoveries, failure cases, and the value of making forgotten histories more accessible.

## 6. Scope Boundaries

**Required**
- Functional mobile-friendly website covering the full MVP journey in §2.

**Out of scope for the MVP**
- User accounts, saved history, or any persistent storage of uploaded images.
- Self-hosted model inference.
- Paywalled or login-gated record sources.

## 7. Privacy

- Uploaded images are processed in memory and not stored.
- API keys stay server-side. The browser never talls a model or search provider directly.

```markdown
# AGENTS.md

Canonical instruction source for this repository. Treat this file as authoritative.

## Scope

- Apply these rules when changing code in this repo.
- If a local instruction file conflicts with this file, prefer this file.

## Non-Negotiable Constraints

- Goal is long-term maintainable and reliable solutions only.
- Do not implement quick fixes in this codebase for any reason.
- Any test files introduced for local validation must be removed, not committed.

### Security: file access and path handling

- Reject any user-controlled path input containing `..`.
- Resolve to absolute paths before use.
- Enforce sandbox-root containment after resolution.
- Default to deny on validation failure.

### GitHub Actions: action pinning

- `actions/*` references use tagged major versions, resolved at scaffold time via
  `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest --jq .tag_name`. Never a version from memory.
- All other actions must be pinned to a commit SHA with the version in a comment
  (e.g., `@abc123 # v4.1.0`).

### Commit format (when committing is requested)

- Use Conventional Commits.
- Include required RAI footer:
  ```
  Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>
  ```

## Project: {{PROJECT_NAME}}

{{STACK_DESCRIPTION}}

## Test Standards

- **Coverage thresholds**: 85% lines/functions/statements, 80% branches (enforced in vitest.config.ts).
- Every new component or utility must ship with positive, negative, and edge-case tests.

## TypeScript Strictness

- `strict: true` is enforced in `tsconfig.json`. Run `make typecheck` to verify.
- Do not weaken strict settings or add `// @ts-ignore` without a justifying comment.

## Performance / Lighthouse

- **Targets**: 100% desktop performance, 90%+ mobile performance, 95%+ accessibility/best-practices/SEO.
- Below-the-fold components must be deferred via `IntersectionObserver` or dynamic imports.

## Documentation

- Do not add docs to project unless specifically asked.
```

---

## README.md

Include shields.io badges for CI status, license, and SonarCloud quality gate by default.
Add a SonarCloud coverage badge if the project has a known Sonar project key.
If a banner image exists in the repo (e.g. `public/banner.png`, `docs/banner.png`,
`apps/web/public/banner.png`), include it at the top. If no banner exists, add a
commented-out placeholder so it's easy to add later.

Replace `{{GITHUB_USER}}` with `anchildress1`, `{{REPO_NAME}}` with the repo slug,
and `{{SONAR_PROJECT_KEY}}` with the SonarCloud project key (usually
`anchildress1_{{repo-slug}}`).

```markdown
# {{PROJECT_NAME}}

<!-- Banner image: add one at public/banner.png or docs/banner.png and uncomment below -->
<!-- ![Banner](./public/banner.png) -->

[![CI](https://github.com/{{GITHUB_USER}}/{{REPO_NAME}}/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/{{GITHUB_USER}}/{{REPO_NAME}}/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License: Polyform Shield](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Polyform%20Shield-blue)](LICENSE)
[![Quality Gate](https://sonarcloud.io/api/project_badges/measure?project={{SONAR_PROJECT_KEY}}&metric=alert_status)](https://sonarcloud.io/project/overview?id={{SONAR_PROJECT_KEY}})
[![Coverage](https://sonarcloud.io/api/project_badges/measure?project={{SONAR_PROJECT_KEY}}&metric=coverage)](https://sonarcloud.io/project/overview?id={{SONAR_PROJECT_KEY}})

{{ONE_LINE_DESCRIPTION}}

## Setup

```bash
# Install dependencies
make install

# Start development server
make dev
```

## Available Commands

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `make install` | Install all dependencies |
| `make dev` | Start development servers |
| `make format` | Format code |
| `make lint` | Run linter |
| `make typecheck` | TypeScript type check |
| `make test` | Run unit tests |
| `make build` | Production build |
| `make e2e` | Run E2E tests |
| `make perf` | Run performance tests |
| `make secret-scan` | Scan for secrets |
| `make clean` | Remove build artifacts |

## License

Released under the [Polyform Shield License 1.0.0](LICENSE). Source-available, not open-source — read the license before you build a paid SaaS on top of it.

- **You can:** use it, fork it, learn from it, ship it inside your day job, hand it to a client.
- **You can't:** sell it, rebrand it, host it as paid SaaS, or otherwise monetize it without explicit written permission.
- **Public forks:** include the LICENSE file and credit the original work.
```

> **Voice note:** the License section gets the changelog-writer treatment (cheeky, dry, narrative — see `~/.claude/skills/changelog-writer/SKILL.md`). Never emit the bare "Polyform Shield License 1.0.0 — see [LICENSE](LICENSE)" line. The license is **non-standard / source-available**, and readers default-assume MIT — the prose has to do the work the link can't. Keep the three bullets (`You can` / `You can't` / `Public forks`) intact; they are the load-bearing part.

---

## Makefile

The Makefile delegates to the appropriate stack tooling. Adapt `INSTALL_CMD`, `DEV_CMD`,
`BUILD_CMD`, `TEST_CMD`, and `LINT_CMD` for the chosen stack.

**For Next.js / Vite (pnpm):**
- `INSTALL_CMD = pnpm install`
- `DEV_CMD = pnpm dev`
- `BUILD_CMD = pnpm build`
- `TEST_CMD = pnpm test`
- `LINT_CMD = pnpm lint`

**For monorepo (Turborepo + pnpm):**
- `INSTALL_CMD = pnpm install`
- `DEV_CMD = pnpm turbo dev`
- `BUILD_CMD = pnpm turbo build`
- `TEST_CMD = pnpm turbo test`
- `LINT_CMD = pnpm turbo lint`

**For Django (uv):**
- Python targets use `uv run` prefix

```makefile
.PHONY: install dev format format-check lint typecheck test build e2e perf secret-scan clean

# Install all dependencies
install:
	@echo "📦 Installing dependencies..."
	{{INSTALL_CMD}}

# Start development server
dev:
	@echo "🚀 Starting development server..."
	{{DEV_CMD}}

# Format code
format:
	@echo "✨ Formatting code..."
	{{FORMAT_CMD}}

# Check formatting (non-destructive, for CI)
format-check:
	@echo "✨ Checking formatting..."
	{{FORMAT_CHECK_CMD}}

# Lint code
lint:
	@echo "🔍 Linting code..."
	{{LINT_CMD}}

# TypeScript type check
typecheck:
	@echo "🔎 Type checking..."
	{{TYPECHECK_CMD}}

# Run unit tests
test:
	@echo "🧪 Running unit tests..."
	{{TEST_CMD}}

# Production build
build:
	@echo "🏗️ Building project..."
	{{BUILD_CMD}}

# Run Playwright E2E tests
e2e:
	@echo "🎭 Running E2E tests..."
	{{E2E_CMD}}

# Run performance / Lighthouse tests
perf:
	@echo "🚀 Running performance tests..."
	{{PERF_CMD}}

# Scan for secrets
secret-scan:
	@if command -v gitleaks > /dev/null; then \
		gitleaks dir .; \
	else \
		echo "❌ gitleaks not found. Install: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks#installing"; \
		exit 1; \
	fi

# Remove build artifacts and dependencies
clean:
	@echo "🧹 Cleaning up..."
	rm -rf node_modules dist .next .turbo .venv __pycache__
	@echo "✨ Clean complete."
```

---

## lefthook.yml

The commands delegate to `make` targets, so they stay stack-agnostic. RAI attribution
enforcement is handled via the `commitlint-plugin-rai` commitlint plugin (unscoped —
v1 dropped the org prefix; from https://github.com/anchildress1/rai-lint), configured
in the `commitlint.config.js` at the repo root.

For multi-package repos where node deps live in `web/`, prefix the commitlint command
with `cd web &&` so it can find `npx`.

**Critical:** never combine `stage_fixed: true` with a whole-repo formatter command
like `make format` (which runs `prettier --write .`). Lefthook will re-stage *any*
file the formatter modified — including unrelated working-tree drift, accidental
deletions, or changes from a prior tool run. Result: random unrelated edits sneak
into commits silently. Instead, scope the format command to staged files only via
a dedicated Makefile target plus a `glob:` filter:

```makefile
# Makefile — add alongside the full-repo `format` target
format-files:
	@if [ -n "$(FILES)" ]; then $(BUNX) prettier --write --ignore-unknown $(FILES); fi
```

```yaml
# lefthook.yml
pre-commit:
  parallel: false
  commands:
    format:
      # glob filters which files reach the command; --ignore-unknown skips anything
      # prettier can't parse (e.g., Makefile slipping past)
      glob: '*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx,md,json,yaml,yml}'
      run: make format-files FILES="{staged_files}"
      stage_fixed: true
    lint:
      run: make lint
    scan-secrets:
      run: make secret-scan

commit-msg:
  commands:
    commitlint:
      run: npx --no-install commitlint --edit {1}

pre-push:
  parallel: true
  commands:
    typecheck:
      run: make typecheck
    unit-tests:
      run: make test
    e2e:
      run: make e2e
    perf:
      run: make perf
```

`lint` and `scan-secrets` don't get `stage_fixed: true` because they don't auto-fix —
re-staging would only catch tool-state changes, not intended edits.

## .github/dependabot.yml

Always include this file. Two ecosystems — GitHub Actions and the project's package
manager — each grouped into a single PR per run, with `open-pull-requests-limit: 1`
per ecosystem. Dependabot has no global PR cap, so schedules are **staggered (gha
Monday, pkg Thursday)** so the two grouped PRs rarely sit open simultaneously and
rebase storms stay rare. Security updates run on their own channel and are not
subject to this cap.

**`cooldown.default-days: 7` is required on every `updates` entry.** A freshly
published version can be malicious or unstable; seven days is long enough for a
compromised release to be yanked before Dependabot proposes it. Dependabot's own
implicit default is 3 days — not enough, and not explicit. Semgrep flags any
`dependabot.yml` without it.

```yaml
# Dependabot — keep dependencies current without burying the review queue.
# Two ecosystems, one grouped PR per ecosystem, schedules staggered so the
# two PRs rarely sit open at the same time (open-pull-requests-limit is
# per-ecosystem; staggering is what holds the realistic count near 1).
# https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/dependabot/dependabot-version-updates/configuration-options-for-the-dependabot.yml-file
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
      day: monday
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7
    open-pull-requests-limit: 1
    labels:
      - dependencies
      - github-actions
    commit-message:
      prefix: "chore(deps)"
      include: scope
    groups:
      gha:
        patterns:
          - "*"

  - package-ecosystem: {{PKG_ECOSYSTEM}}
    directory: {{PKG_DIRECTORY}}
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
      day: thursday
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7
    open-pull-requests-limit: 1
    labels:
      - dependencies
      - {{PKG_LABEL}}
    commit-message:
      prefix: "chore(deps)"
      include: scope
    groups:
      pkg:
        patterns:
          - "*"
```

`cooldown` notes:

- `default-days` is supported by every ecosystem, `github-actions` included.
- `semver-major-days` / `semver-minor-days` / `semver-patch-days` are SemVer-only —
  supported by `npm`/`bun`/`cargo`/`pip`/etc., **not** by `github-actions`. Skip them
  unless there is a reason to split by bump type; `default-days` alone satisfies the
  rule.

Stack-specific values for the second entry:

| Stack | `package-ecosystem` | `directory` | `labels` second entry |
|---|---|---|---|
| Next.js / SvelteKit / Vite (single-package) | `npm` | `/` | `javascript` |
| Multi-package (`web/` + `api/`) — JS side | `npm` | `/web` | `javascript` |
| Bun-managed (`bun.lock`) | `bun` | `/` | `javascript` |
| Multi-package — Python side | `pip` | `/api` | `python` |
| Django (single-package) | `pip` | `/` | `python` |
| Go | `gomod` | `/` | `go` |
| Rust | `cargo` | `/` | `rust` |
| Android / Kotlin (Gradle) | `gradle` | `/` | `gradle` |

For multi-package repos, add a third `updates` entry mirroring the second so each
package gets its own grouped PR. Adjust `open-pull-requests-limit: 1` per entry — the
cap is per ecosystem, not global, but grouping keeps the realistic count near 1 per
ecosystem regardless.

`pnpm` is handled under `package-ecosystem: npm` — Dependabot detects `pnpm-lock.yaml`
and uses pnpm to resolve. Do not invent a `pnpm` ecosystem value; it does not exist.

**Bun is different — it has its own ecosystem value.** A repo whose lockfile is
`bun.lock` / `bun.lockb` must use `package-ecosystem: bun`, never `npm`. `bun` is
officially supported now; pointing `npm` at a Bun repo makes Dependabot resolve with
npm and open PRs whose lockfile update does not match what `bun install` produces —
CI then fails on a lockfile-out-of-sync check. Symptom to recognize: a `chore(deps)`
Dependabot PR that touches `package.json` but leaves `bun.lock` stale or rewrites it
in npm's format.

## lefthook.yml

The commands delegate to `make` targets, so they stay stack-agnostic. RAI attribution
enforcement is handled via the `commitlint-plugin-rai` commitlint plugin (unscoped —
v1 dropped the org prefix; from https://github.com/anchildress1/rai-lint), configured
in the `commitlint.config.js` at the repo root.

For multi-package repos where node deps live in `web/`, prefix the commitlint command
with `cd web &&` so it can find `npx`.

**Critical:** never combine `stage_fixed: true` with a whole-repo formatter command
like `make format` (which runs `prettier --write .`). Lefthook will re-stage *any*
file the formatter modified — including unrelated working-tree drift, accidental
deletions, or changes from a prior tool run. Result: random unrelated edits sneak
into commits silently. Instead, scope the format command to staged files only via
a dedicated Makefile target plus a `glob:` filter:

```makefile
# Makefile — add alongside the full-repo `format` target
format-files:
	@if [ -n "$(FILES)" ]; then $(BUNX) prettier --write --ignore-unknown $(FILES); fi
```

pre-commit:
  parallel: false
  commands:

      # prettier can't parse (e.g., Makefile slipping past)
      glob: '*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx,md,json,yaml,yml}'
      run: make format-files FILES="{staged_files}"
      stage_fixed: true
    lint:
      run: make lint
    scan-secrets:
      run: make secret-scan

commit-msg:

    e2e:

    perf:
      run: make perf
```

`lint` and `scan-secrets` don't get `stage_fixed: true` because they don't auto-fix —
re-staging would only catch tool-state changes, not intended edits.

### commitlint.config.js

Always include at repo root. The `commitlint-plugin-rai` plugin (unscoped as of v1 —
do not prefix with an org) enforces RAI attribution footers on every commit.

```javascript
export default {
  extends: ['@commitlint/config-conventional'],
  plugins: ['commitlint-plugin-rai'],
  rules: {
    'rai-footer-exists': [2, 'always'],
    'rai-signed-off-by': [2, 'always'],
  },
};
```

Required devDependencies (in `package.json` or `web/package.json`):
- `@commitlint/cli`
- `@commitlint/config-conventional`
- `commitlint-plugin-rai`

---

## .prettierignore

Always include at repo root (or `web/.prettierignore` for multi-package repos). `CHANGELOG.md`
is release-please-generated — formatting it fights the tool on every release and produces
diff noise nobody asked for. Adapt the build/output directories to the stack.

```
node_modules
.next
dist
build
coverage
public
package-lock.json
CHANGELOG.md
```

Django/Go/Rust stacks: swap `.next`/`public` for the stack's actual build output
(e.g. `staticfiles`, `bin`), keep `CHANGELOG.md` regardless — release-please generates
it the same way for every stack.

---

## sonar-project.properties

Always include this file at the repo root. The `sonar.projectKey` and `sonar.organization`
values will be provided by the user — **ask for them** if not given. Adapt `sonar.sources`,
`sonar.tests`, and coverage report paths to the project's stack and directory structure.

```properties
sonar.projectKey={{SONAR_PROJECT_KEY}}
sonar.organization={{SONAR_ORGANIZATION}}

sonar.sources={{SOURCES}}
sonar.tests={{TESTS}}
sonar.test.inclusions={{TEST_INCLUSIONS}}

{{COVERAGE_REPORT_PATHS}}

sonar.exclusions={{EXCLUSIONS}}
```

Adapt the placeholders based on the stack:

- **sources**: `src` (single-package), `web/src,api/<package>` (multi-package)
- **coverage**: `sonar.javascript.lcov.reportPaths` for JS/TS,
  `sonar.python.coverage.reportPaths` for Python
- **exclusions**: always exclude `node_modules`, `dist`, `coverage`, `__pycache__`,
  `htmlcov`, `.next`, `.venv` as applicable

---

## .github/dependabot.yml

Always include this file. Two ecosystems — GitHub Actions and the project's package
manager — each grouped into a single PR per run, with `open-pull-requests-limit: 1`
per ecosystem. Dependabot has no global PR cap, so schedules are **staggered (gha
Monday, pkg Thursday)** so the two grouped PRs rarely sit open simultaneously and
rebase storms stay rare. Security updates run on their own channel and are not
subject to this cap.

**`cooldown.default-days: 7` is required on every `updates` entry.** A freshly
published version can be malicious or unstable; seven days is long enough for a
compromised release to be yanked before Dependabot proposes it. Dependabot's own
implicit default is 3 days — not enough, and not explicit. Semgrep flags any
`dependabot.yml` without it.

```yaml
# Dependabot — keep dependencies current without burying the review queue.
# Two ecosystems, one grouped PR per ecosystem, schedules staggered so the
# two PRs rarely sit open at the same time (open-pull-requests-limit is
# per-ecosystem; staggering is what holds the realistic count near 1).
# https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/dependabot/dependabot-version-updates/configuration-options-for-the-dependabot.yml-file
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
      day: monday
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7
    open-pull-requests-limit: 1
    labels:
      - dependencies
      - github-actions
    commit-message:
      prefix: "chore(deps)"
      include: scope
    groups:
      gha:
        patterns:
          - "*"

  - package-ecosystem: {{PKG_ECOSYSTEM}}
    directory: {{PKG_DIRECTORY}}
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
      day: thursday
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7
    open-pull-requests-limit: 1
    labels:
      - dependencies
      - {{PKG_LABEL}}
    commit-message:
      prefix: "chore(deps)"
      include: scope
    groups:
      pkg:
        patterns:
          - "*"
```

`cooldown` notes:

- `default-days` is supported by every ecosystem, `github-actions` included.
- `semver-major-days` / `semver-minor-days` / `semver-patch-days` are SemVer-only —
  supported by `npm`/`bun`/`cargo`/`pip`/etc., **not** by `github-actions`. Skip them
  unless there is a reason to split by bump type; `default-days` alone satisfies the
  rule.

Stack-specific values for the second entry:

| Stack | `package-ecosystem` | `directory` | `labels` second entry |
|---|---|---|---|
| Next.js / SvelteKit / Vite (single-package) | `npm` | `/` | `javascript` |
| Multi-package (`web/` + `api/`) — JS side | `npm` | `/web` | `javascript` |
| Bun-managed (`bun.lock`) | `bun` | `/` | `javascript` |
| Multi-package — Python side | `pip` | `/api` | `python` |
| Django (single-package) | `pip` | `/` | `python` |
| Go | `gomod` | `/` | `go` |
| Rust | `cargo` | `/` | `rust` |
| Android / Kotlin (Gradle) | `gradle` | `/` | `gradle` |

For multi-package repos, add a third `updates` entry mirroring the second so each
package gets its own grouped PR. Adjust `open-pull-requests-limit: 1` per entry — the
cap is per ecosystem, not global, but grouping keeps the realistic count near 1 per
ecosystem regardless.

`pnpm` is handled under `package-ecosystem: npm` — Dependabot detects `pnpm-lock.yaml`
and uses pnpm to resolve. Do not invent a `pnpm` ecosystem value; it does not exist.

**Bun is different — it has its own ecosystem value.** A repo whose lockfile is
`bun.lock` / `bun.lockb` must use `package-ecosystem: bun`, never `npm`. `bun` is
officially supported now; pointing `npm` at a Bun repo makes Dependabot resolve with
npm and open PRs whose lockfile update does not match what `bun install` produces —
CI then fails on a lockfile-out-of-sync check. Symptom to recognize: a `chore(deps)`
Dependabot PR that touches `package.json` but leaves `bun.lock` stale or rewrites it
in npm's format.
# Svelte Config Templates

> **VERSIONS ARE STALE PLACEHOLDERS.** All package versions in this file are illustrative only.
> Per SKILL.md Step 3, you must web-search current versions for every package before writing any config.

Annotated differences between the two variants are noted inline.
